learningObjectives.title: The Black Death and its impact

questions.q: In which year did the Hundred Years War begin?
questions.explain: The war began in 1337 when Edward III pressed his claim to the French throne.

questions.q: Which English king started the Hundred Years War by claiming the throne of France?
questions.explain: Edward III claimed the French crown through his mother, Isabella of France, triggering the war.

questions.q: At which major 1346 battle did the English longbow secure a famous victory?
questions.explain: The Battle of Crécy in 1346 was a decisive English victory won largely by massed longbowmen.

questions.q: At the Battle of Poitiers in 1356, which French king was taken prisoner by the English?
questions.explain: The Black Prince captured the French king John II at Poitiers in 1356, a huge blow to France.

questions.q: Why was the longbow so effective against French knights?
options: It could fire arrows rapidly over long distances
It was an early gunpowder weapon
It needed no training to use well
It was thrown by hand at close range
questions.explain: Skilled archers could loose many arrows quickly and at range, cutting down cavalry before they reached English lines.

questions.q: What was a 'chevauchée' during the Hundred Years War?
options: A fast-moving raid to devastate enemy land
questions.explain: A chevauchée was a mounted raid designed to burn, loot and terrorise the French countryside and weaken the enemy.

questions.q: Why was the capture of Calais in 1347 so valuable to England?
options: It gave England a fortified port and lasting foothold in France
It was the capital city of France
questions.explain: Calais became a permanent English base for trade and launching campaigns into France for over two centuries.

questions.q: An English commander in 1346 places his archers on high ground to fire volleys at charging French cavalry. Which battle and weapon does this describe?
questions.explain: This describes the English longbowmen who broke the French cavalry charges at Crécy in 1346.

questions.q: In which year did the Black Death first arrive in England?
questions.explain: The plague reached England in 1348, arriving through south-coast ports such as Melcombe in Dorset.

questions.q: What name was given to the painful dark swellings that were a key symptom of the plague?
questions.explain: Buboes were swellings in the neck, armpits and groin, giving the bubonic plague its name.

questions.q: How did the Black Death actually spread, according to modern understanding?
questions.explain: The disease was spread mainly by fleas living on black rats, though people at the time did not know this.

questions.q: What did most people in England at the time believe had caused the Black Death?
options: God's punishment for sin and bad air
questions.explain: Medieval people commonly blamed the plague on God's anger or 'bad air' (miasma), lacking knowledge of germs.

questions.q: Roughly what proportion of England's population is estimated to have died in the Black Death?
options: Between a third and a half
questions.explain: Historians estimate that roughly a third to a half of England's people died in the outbreak of 1348-49.

questions.q: Why were surviving peasants able to demand higher wages after the Black Death?
options: A severe labour shortage gave them more bargaining power
The king ordered all wages to be doubled
There was a huge surplus of workers
questions.explain: With so many workers dead, labour was scarce, so survivors could demand better pay and conditions.

questions.q: Why did the government introduce the Statute of Labourers in 1351?
options: To hold wages down to their pre-plague levels
To free all serfs from their lords
To raise money for the Black Death cure
To pay soldiers fighting in France
questions.explain: The Statute of Labourers tried to fix wages at pre-plague rates and stop workers moving for higher pay.

questions.q: A landowner in 1352 complains he cannot find enough workers and that those available demand double the old pay. Which event best explains his problem?
options: The Black Death had killed much of the workforce
A new war had drafted all peasants
A good harvest had made peasants rich
The Statute of Labourers had freed the serfs
questions.explain: The huge death toll from the plague left a labour shortage, allowing workers to demand higher wages.

questions.q: In which year did the Peasants' Revolt take place?
questions.explain: The Peasants' Revolt broke out in 1381, chiefly among rebels from Kent and Essex.

questions.q: Who was the main leader of the rebels from Kent during the Peasants' Revolt?
questions.explain: Wat Tyler emerged as the chief leader of the Kentish rebels who marched on London in 1381.

questions.q: Which radical preacher, linked to the revolt, asked 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'
questions.explain: The preacher John Ball used this famous saying to argue that all people were originally equal.

questions.q: Why did the Poll Tax cause such anger among ordinary people in 1381?
options: It was a flat-rate tax that hit the poor far harder than the rich
Only wealthy nobles were required to pay it
It funded a cure for the Black Death
It was paid entirely in livestock
questions.explain: The third Poll Tax charged everyone the same flat sum, placing a much heavier burden on poorer households.

questions.q: A chronicle records rebels burning the Savoy Palace in London in 1381. Whose property was it, and why was it a target?
options: John of Gaunt's, as he was a hated royal figure blamed for misrule
The King's own palace, attacked to seize the crown
Wat Tyler's, destroyed by loyal townsfolk
A monastery, burned for its wealth
questions.explain: The Savoy belonged to John of Gaunt, whom rebels blamed for corrupt government and the hated taxes.
